[THOUGHT] The patient is a stable 32-year-old woman with sudden onset left lower quadrant abdominal pain during physical exertion (kickboxing). Exam shows localized tenderness and guarding in the left lower quadrant. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a large amount of free fluid in the rectouterine pouch (Pouch of Douglas), consistent with intraperitoneal fluid—most likely blood in this setting. Urine pregnancy test is negative, making ectopic pregnancy unlikely. CBC is reported normal, but early bleeding may not yet have produced anemia or hematocrit changes. The clinical picture—sudden unilateral pelvic pain provoked by exertion/trauma, localized tenderness, and significant pelvic free fluid—most closely fits an acute rupture of an ovarian cyst with hemoperitoneum, classically a hemorrhagic (including corpus luteum) cyst rupture. Ovarian torsion is less likely because the key finding here is large free fluid suggesting rupture/bleeding; ectopic pregnancy is unlikely with a negative hCG. Splenic injury would more likely cause LUQ/shoulder symptoms and be investigated with abdominal (not pelvic) imaging. Therefore the single most likely diagnosis is a ruptured hemorrhagic ovarian cyst on the left with resultant pelvic hemoperitoneum.
